Francis I. From 1494 to 1547, he was the first French Renaissance king, a patron of arts and letters who made France a cultural power and rival to the Holy Roman Empire. His reign balanced military ambition against the patronage of humanist scholars and artists, including Leonardo da Vinci himself.

During his 32-year reign from 1515 to 1547, Francis declared himself Father and Restorer of Letters. He welcomed scholars, artists, and printers to his court, spreading Renaissance ideals across France and fundamentally transforming the kingdom's cultural life. He brought Leonardo da Vinci to live and work in France, cementing his reputation as a maker and patron of culture, and Leonardo spent his final years under Francis's protection.

Yet Francis was no mere patron. He waged the Italian Wars against Charles V and the Holy Roman Empire, competing fiercely for dominance in Italy and European prestige. The great military setback came at the Battle of Pavia in 1525, when he was captured and forced to ransom himself. Despite this defeat, he continued to project French power and ambition across Europe.

Francis proved politically shrewd as well. He negotiated the Concordat of Bologna with the Pope in 1516, granting the French crown significant control over church appointments and revenues in France. This agreement shifted ecclesiastical authority in France toward the monarchy. He also built and expanded magnificent châteaux like Fontainebleau, architectural masterpieces that became showcases of Renaissance taste and royal power.

His reign marked France's transition from medieval to Renaissance culture and established it as a major artistic and intellectual center of Europe.
